Chapter 8: The World’s Common Ground—English Goes Global
By the time the twentieth century rolled around, English was more than just the language of one country.
Wars, international trade, and the exchange of ideas sent English traveling—spreading to every corner of the planet.
Imagine classrooms in India or Nigeria, where kids would learn English right alongside their own native tongues. Or offices buzzing in Tokyo, markets bustling in Nairobi—English became the go-to language for doing business and making connections.
For a lot of people, picking up English meant opportunity. Picture a student in Hong Kong, staying up late, pouring over English textbooks, all for a shot at studying abroad.
Or a nurse in Kenya, using English to care for patients who speak all sorts of languages.
English opened doors, but it also brought new challenges. Some folks started to worry—would their local languages fade away? Would everything start sounding the same?
But here’s the thing: English didn’t just take over. It learned to adapt.
In India, it morphed into Hinglish—a playful blend of English and Hindi, packed with inside jokes and clever turns of phrase.
In Singapore, locals created Singlish, with its own rhythm and unique rules.
And in Jamaica, English mixed with African and Caribbean languages, becoming something completely original.
Just think—a taxi driver in Lagos might flip between English and Yoruba in the middle of a conversation, without even pausing.
Or a teenager in Manila, texting friends in a mashup of English and Tagalog.
At this point, English wasn’t just British or American anymore—it belonged to everyone who used it.
Of course, the rise of English around the world brought up some big questions.
Who gets to decide what’s “correct”? Whose accent should be the standard?
Most people didn’t lose sleep over it—they just spoke however worked best, mixing, borrowing, and inventing as they went.
In the end, it became clear: English isn’t just one thing. It’s a whole family of languages, each with its own flavor and its own story to tell.
The adventure of English had gone global—shaped by millions of voices, and still growing every single day.
